title: Choosing the Graft: Marrow, Mobilized Blood or Cord
summary: Compare bone marrow, mobilized blood and cord blood as stem-cell sources, explain G-CSF and plerixafor mobilization and the T-cell depletion trade-off, and process ABO-mismatched grafts safely.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 43 Hit 7 (G-CSF and plerixafor mobilization), Hit 9 (cord blood), Hit 10 (blood vs marrow), Hit 11 (T-cell depletion), Hit 12 (ABO-incompatible grafts), Hit 14 (reinfusion reactions) and Traps 4–6. Checked against Alipourfard 2026, Anasetti 2012, Nunn 2026, Koster 2024, Bleakley 2022 (abstract), Matteocci 2024 and Niebergall-Roth 2025. The reviewer gives G-CSF as 5–10 µg/kg for 4–5 days; the source read gives 10 µg/kg/day for 4–6 days with apheresis on day 5. Hit 12’s “HPCs do not express ABO antigens” conflicts with Matteocci 2024 (register flag rv-hpc-abo); the lesson teaches only that ABO mismatch is not a contraindication. Not taught: chemotherapy mobilization timing, plerixafor side effects, cord volume cut-offs, 2017 graft-source percentages and the CAR-T approvals (Hit 13).

objectives: Explain how G-CSF and plerixafor mobilize stem cells into the blood.
Compare mobilized blood, bone marrow and cord blood grafts for engraftment, GVHD and matching.
Explain the T-cell depletion trade-off between GVHD and relapse.
Choose red-cell or plasma depletion for major or minor ABO-mismatched grafts and recognize DMSO infusion reactions.

scenes.title: Three bags, one patient
scenes.altText: A patient card: adult with acute leukemia, blood group O, needs an allogeneic transplant. Three source bins appear: Bone marrow, Mobilized blood, Cord blood. A donor card: group A. Question tokens: “Which source?”, “What about the A red cells?”. The cartoon scientist looks between the bins.

cues.text: An adult with leukemia, blood group O, needs a stem-cell transplant from a donor.
The stem cells can come from bone marrow, from blood after mobilization, or from umbilical cord blood. Each choice has a trade-off.
And the matched donor is group A. Does that block the transplant, and what must the lab do to the bag?

props.label: What about the A red cells?

scenes.title: Mobilization: cutting the marrow’s tether
scenes.altText: A marrow card holds stem-cell tokens tethered by “CXCR4 ↔ CXCL12 (SDF-1)”. A G-CSF token arrives (10 µg/kg/day for 4–6 days); a protease token cuts the tether and the stem-cell tokens slide right into a “Blood” card; an apheresis token appears at day 5. A plerixafor token blocks CXCR4 directly; a result card: with G-CSF in a lymphoma trial, ≥ 5 × 10⁶ CD34⁺/kg was reached in 70% vs 34% with G-CSF alone.

cues.text: Stem cells live in a marrow niche. The CXCR4 receptor on the stem cell holds onto CXCL12, also called SDF-1, like a tether.
G-CSF, given at about 10 micrograms per kilogram per day for 4 to 6 days, makes marrow cells release proteases that break down SDF-1.
With the tether cut, stem cells spill into the blood, and apheresis collects them, usually starting on day 5.
Some patients mobilize poorly. Plerixafor blocks CXCR4 directly and is added to G-CSF.
In a lymphoma trial, G-CSF plus plerixafor reached the target CD34 dose in 70 percent of patients, versus 34 percent with G-CSF alone.

scenes.title: Trade-offs: speed, GVHD, matching and T cells
scenes.altText: Three cards fill in. “Blood vs marrow (unrelated donors, randomized trial)”: neutrophils engraft 5 days sooner and platelets 7 days sooner with blood; graft failure 3% vs 9%; chronic GVHD at 2 years 53% vs 41%; 2-year survival similar. “Cord blood”: tolerates more HLA mismatch, available immediately, less chronic GVHD; low cell dose → slower engraftment; ex vivo expansion and double cords extend adult use. “T-cell depletion”: less severe GVHD but more relapse, because the graft-versus-leukemia effect falls; donor lymphocyte infusion can boost it later.

cues.text: Mobilized blood versus marrow, from a randomized trial of unrelated donors. With blood, neutrophils engraft about 5 days sooner and platelets about 7 days sooner.
Blood grafts failed less often, 3 versus 9 percent, but caused more chronic GVHD, 53 versus 41 percent at two years. Survival was similar.
Cord blood tolerates more HLA mismatch, is available at once, and causes less chronic GVHD. Its weakness is a small cell dose, so engraftment is slower.
That is why cord was limited in adults. Ex vivo expansion and double-cord grafts are partly overcoming it.
Removing T cells from a graft lowers severe GVHD but raises relapse: the same donor T cells fight the leukemia. That is the graft-versus-leukemia effect.

scenes.title: ABO-mismatched bags and the thaw
scenes.altText: A card: “ABO incompatibility is not a contraindication to transplant.” Major mismatch (group O recipient, group A donor): recipient anti-A meets donor A red cells → red-cell depletion of marrow grafts with > 20 mL of red cells; blood grafts usually carry < 20 mL; later risk: delayed hemolysis and pure red cell aplasia. Minor mismatch (group O donor, group A recipient): donor anti-A plasma → plasma depletion if the anti-recipient titer is ≥ 256; later risk: passenger lymphocyte syndrome. Then a thaw card: DMSO (up to ~1 g/kg accepted) causes histamine-related reactions — chills, nausea and vomiting, blood pressure and heart-rate changes, cough and dyspnea, rarely neurologic events; premedicate and start the infusion slowly.

cues.text: ABO mismatch does not stop a stem-cell transplant. Donor choice rests on HLA. But the bag still contains red cells and plasma.
Major mismatch: a group O recipient has anti-A, and the group A donor bag has A red cells. Marrow grafts with more than 20 milliliters of red cells are red-cell depleted.
Minor mismatch is the reverse: donor plasma carries antibody against the recipient’s cells. The plasma is removed when the titer is high.
Watch later, too: pure red cell aplasia after major mismatch, and passenger lymphocyte hemolysis after minor mismatch.
At thaw, DMSO is not inert. It releases histamine: chills, nausea, blood pressure swings and dyspnea. Premedicate and start slowly.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards appear in turn: “Removing T cells lowers relapse because GVHD is gone” (✓ relapse rises — graft-versus-leukemia is lost); “Cord’s looser matching makes it ideal for adults” (✓ the small cell dose limits adults; expansion helps); “DMSO is inert” (✓ histamine-release reactions — premedicate, infuse slowly).

cues.text: Trap one: removing T cells lowers relapse because GVHD is gone. No. Relapse rises, because the graft-versus-leukemia effect is lost.
Trap two: cord blood’s looser matching makes it ideal for adults. No. Its small cell dose slows engraftment; expansion helps.
Trap three: DMSO is inert. No. It releases histamine and causes infusion reactions, so premedicate and infuse slowly.

props.title: ✗ “T-cell depletion lowers relapse — GVHD is gone.”
✗ “Looser matching makes cord ideal for adults.”
lines: ✓ Small cell dose limits adults · expansion helps

scenes.title: Blood is fast, marrow is gentle, cord is forgiving
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Blood is fast, marrow is gentle, cord is forgiving — but small.” Three tokens: blood = fastest engraftment, more chronic GVHD; marrow = less chronic GVHD, more graft failure; cord = tolerates mismatch, small dose. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: blood is fast, marrow is gentle, cord is forgiving but small. Blood engrafts fastest, marrow causes less chronic GVHD, and cord tolerates mismatch but has few cells.

Where it breaks: results depend on donor type and GVHD prevention, such as post-transplant cyclophosphamide; newer selective T-cell depletion may avoid the relapse penalty; and cord expansion is changing the cell-dose limit.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Blood: faster engraftment, more chronic GVHD · cord: tolerant but small · T-cell depletion: GVHD ↓, relapse ↑”, “ABO mismatch is allowed: major → RBC depletion, minor → plasma depletion · DMSO reactions: premedicate”.

cues.text: Mobilized blood engrafts fastest but causes more chronic GVHD, cord tolerates mismatch but has few cells, T-cell depletion trades GVHD for relapse, and ABO mismatch is allowed if the lab removes incompatible red cells or plasma.

props.label: Blood fast, more cGVHD · cord tolerant but small · T-cell depletion: GVHD ↓ relapse ↑
ABO mismatch allowed: major → RBC depletion · minor → plasma depletion · DMSO: premedicate

explanation.what: Plain language: stem cells can be taken from marrow, coaxed into the blood and collected, or banked from cord blood; each source trades speed, GVHD risk and cell dose. Scientific terms: G-CSF mobilization, plerixafor (CXCR4 antagonist), PB-HPC vs BM-HPC, umbilical cord blood (UCB), T-cell depletion (TCD), graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), graft-versus-leukemia (GVL), major and minor ABO incompatibility, DMSO cryoprotectant.
explanation.why: CXCR4 on stem cells binds marrow CXCL12 (SDF-1); G-CSF-induced proteases degrade SDF-1 and plerixafor blocks CXCR4, so stem cells leave the marrow. Blood grafts carry more cells and T cells: faster engraftment but more chronic GVHD. Cord blood’s naïve immune cells tolerate HLA mismatch but its cell dose is small. Donor T cells cause GVHD and also kill leukemia.
explanation.measure: G-CSF ≈ 10 µg/kg/day for 4–6 days, apheresis from day 5. Major ABO mismatch: red-cell depletion of marrow grafts with > 20 mL red cells; minor: plasma depletion when anti-recipient titer ≥ 256 (one review’s protocol). DMSO dose up to ~1 g/kg is typically accepted; premedicate and start infusion slowly.
explanation.differs: Major mismatch (recipient antibody vs donor red cells → immediate hemolysis, delayed hemolysis, PRCA) vs minor mismatch (donor antibody vs recipient red cells → immediate hemolysis, passenger lymphocyte syndrome).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: blood vs marrow engraftment and chronic GVHD, cord cell-dose limit, T-cell depletion and relapse, which product manipulation for major vs minor ABO mismatch, and DMSO reactions on reinfusion.

mnemonic.text: Blood is fast, marrow is gentle, cord is forgiving — but small.
mnemonic.explanation: Blood grafts engraft fastest but cause more chronic GVHD; marrow causes less chronic GVHD but fails more often; cord tolerates HLA mismatch but has a small cell dose.
mnemonic.limitation: Results depend on donor type and GVHD prophylaxis (e.g., post-transplant cyclophosphamide); selective naïve T-cell depletion may avoid the relapse penalty; cord expansion is easing the cell-dose limit.

takeaway: Mobilized blood engrafts fastest but causes more chronic GVHD, cord tolerates mismatch but has few cells, T-cell depletion trades GVHD for relapse, and ABO mismatch is allowed if the lab removes incompatible red cells or plasma.

questions.stem: A group O recipient will receive a bone marrow graft from a group A, HLA-matched donor. The product contains 150 mL of red cells. What should the processing laboratory do?

options.text: Red-cell deplete the graft before infusion
options.rationale: Correct. This is a major ABO mismatch: recipient anti-A would hemolyze the donor A red cells, so marrow grafts with > 20 mL of red cells are red-cell depleted.

options.text: Cancel the transplant because ABO groups differ
options.rationale: Incorrect. ABO incompatibility is not a contraindication to stem-cell transplant.
Incorrect. Plasma depletion addresses minor mismatch (donor antibody); here the problem is donor red cells.

options.text: Infuse unchanged; stem cells are not affected by ABO
options.rationale: Incorrect. The red cells in the bag can cause acute hemolysis.

questions.stem: In a randomized trial of unrelated-donor transplants, how did mobilized peripheral blood stem cells compare with bone marrow?

options.text: Faster engraftment and less graft failure, but more chronic GVHD
options.rationale: Correct. Neutrophils engrafted 5 days and platelets 7 days sooner; graft failure 3% vs 9%; chronic GVHD 53% vs 41%.

options.text: Slower engraftment and less chronic GVHD
options.rationale: Incorrect. That describes marrow relative to blood.
Incorrect. Two-year survival was not significantly different.
Incorrect. Engraftment speed, graft failure and chronic GVHD differed.

questions.stem: A transplant program removes T cells from donor grafts. Which outcome should it expect, compared with unmanipulated grafts?

options.text: Less severe GVHD but a higher relapse risk
options.rationale: Correct. The same donor T cells that cause GVHD also provide the graft-versus-leukemia effect.
Incorrect. Losing graft-versus-leukemia raises relapse risk.
Incorrect. Removing T cells lowers GVHD.
Incorrect. T-cell depletion is used precisely to reduce severe GVHD.

references.citation: Almoradie A. MEMORY LAB: The Memory-First Medical Laboratory Science Reviewer. 1st ed., v2.0. 2026. Chapter 43, Stem Cells and Tissue Banking (EPUB; no fixed page numbers).
references.usedFor: Curriculum source: scope and exam framing. Not used as verification.

references.citation: Alipourfard I, Mokhtari T, Lesniak A, Saharkhiz S, Zelazewska Z. Immunomodulatory agents and factors in poor hematopoietic stem cell mobilization: current strategies and future prospects. Stem Cell Rev Rep. 2026;22(3):1127-1138.
references.usedFor: CXCR4–CXCL12 (SDF-1) retains HSCs in the marrow niche; G-CSF releases proteases that degrade SDF-1; G-CSF 10 µg/kg/day for 4–6 days with apheresis on day 5; plerixafor is a selective CXCR4 inhibitor; G-CSF + plerixafor reached ≥ 5 × 10⁶ CD34⁺/kg in 70% vs 34% with G-CSF alone in a phase III NHL study.

references.citation: Anasetti C, Logan BR, Lee SJ, et al. Peripheral-blood stem cells versus bone marrow from unrelated donors. N Engl J Med. 2012;367(16):1487-1496.
references.usedFor: Randomized trial: 2-year survival 51% vs 46% (NS); graft failure 3% vs 9%; chronic GVHD at 2 years 53% vs 41%; median neutrophil engraftment 5 days and platelet engraftment 7 days shorter with PBSC; no difference in acute GVHD or relapse.

references.citation: Nunn J, Poulton K, Wynn R. Don’t cut the cord: why umbilical cord blood still deserves a place in transplantation. Int J Immunogenet. 2026;53(3):229-239.
references.usedFor: UCB permits greater HLA mismatch tolerance, can be accessed immediately and has lower chronic GVHD; challenges are cost and cell dose (TNC/kg correlates with outcome); delayed engraftment; ex vivo expansion is overcoming low cell dose and delayed engraftment for older paediatric and adult recipients.

references.citation: Koster EAS, von dem Borne PA, van Balen P, et al. Risk factors for graft-versus-host-disease after donor lymphocyte infusion following T-cell depleted allogeneic stem cell transplantation. Front Immunol. 2024;15:1335341.
references.usedFor: TCD reduces the risk of severe GvHD but increases relapse risk by reducing the GvL effect; unmodified DLI can be given after alloSCT to boost GvL.

references.citation: Bleakley M, Sehgal A, Seropian S, et al. Naive T-cell depletion to prevent chronic graft-versus-host disease. J Clin Oncol. 2022;40(11):1174-1185.
references.usedFor: Abstract only: naïve T-cell depletion of PBSC grafts gave very low chronic GVHD without apparent excess relapse or nonrelapse mortality.

references.citation: Matteocci A, Pierelli L. Immuno-hematologic complexity of ABO-incompatible allogeneic HSC transplantation. Cells. 2024;13(10):814.
references.usedFor: ABO incompatibility is not a contraindication for HSCT; Table 2: major — RBC depletion of BM grafts (> 20 mL), no RBC manipulation of PBSC grafts (< 20 mL), delayed hemolysis, PRCA; minor — plasma depletion if anti-recipient titer ≥ 1:256, passenger lymphocyte syndrome; states ABO antigens are present on HSCs.

references.citation: Niebergall-Roth E, Kluth MA. Dimethyl sulfoxide in cryopreserved mesenchymal stromal cell therapy products: is there a safety risk to patients? J Transl Med. 2025;23(1):932.
references.usedFor: DMSO-cryopreserved HSC infusions cause reactions mostly attributed to histamine release: chills, GI (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain), cardiopulmonary (hypo/hypertension, brady/tachycardia, cough, dyspnea), neurologic (rare); ~1 g DMSO/kg typically accepted for HSCT; premedication; start infusion slowly.

claims.text: CXCR4–CXCL12 retains HSCs; G-CSF proteases degrade SDF-1; G-CSF 10 µg/kg/day × 4–6 d, apheresis day 5; plerixafor blocks CXCR4; 70% vs 34% target reached.
PB vs BM (unrelated): engraftment 5 d / 7 d sooner; graft failure 3% vs 9%; chronic GVHD 53% vs 41%; survival similar.
Cord: more HLA mismatch tolerated, immediate availability, less chronic GVHD; low cell dose → delayed engraftment; expansion extending use.
T-cell depletion lowers severe GVHD but raises relapse (GVL loss); DLI boosts GVL; selective naïve T-cell depletion may avoid excess relapse.
ABO mismatch not a contraindication; major → RBC depletion of BM > 20 mL; minor → plasma depletion if titer ≥ 256; PRCA and passenger lymphocyte syndrome.
DMSO infusion reactions from histamine release; ~1 g/kg accepted; premedicate, start slowly.
HPCs do not express ABO antigens; plerixafor’s main side effect is GI irritation; cord collections < 40 mL are discarded.
claims.note: Not taught. Matteocci 2024 states ABO antigens are present on HSCs (register flag rv-hpc-abo); the other details were not in the sources read.
